title: The Journal is a program
summary: The Model you just built is also a script: export it, edit one line by hand, replay it, and get the study you meant instead of the one you happened to click.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: Every Command lands in the Journal the instant it runs, whether you clicked it, typed it, or asked the Assistant. `model.new` is the first one, same as always.

steps.title: The beam
steps.explain: The same 1 m steel beam as the `cantilever` tutorial. You already know these Commands; what this page is about is what they add up to once they're all in the Journal together.

steps.title: Assign it
steps.explain: One Material on the one Body.

steps.title: Load the tip
steps.explain: 1 kN down at the free end.

steps.title: Solve it
steps.explain: Ten Commands, in order — and that list is not a log of what you did, it is the Model. Replay it from empty and you get this exact Model back, every time, on any host.

steps.title: Export it as a script
steps.explain: Open the Script tab — `query.script` — and the ten Commands you just ran come back as a small TypeScript program against the `fem` API, one line per Command: `await fem.geometry.addBox({ name: "beam", size: ["1 m", "100 mm", "100 mm"] });`, on down to `await fem.solve.run({ step: "static" });`. This is not a summary of the Model. It is the Model — every argument you typed, byte for byte.

steps.title: Edit one line
steps.explain: Press "edit this script" and the same text becomes an editable draft. Change the beam's `size` from `["1 m", "100 mm", "100 mm"]` to `["2 m", "100 mm", "100 mm"]` — one keystroke, no palette, no form — and nothing else in the script has to change: every later line still just refers to whatever `beam` turns out to be.

steps.title: Replay it
steps.explain: Press ▶ Run script. The engine dispatches every line from the top — a fresh `model.new`, the edited `geometry.addBox`, and on down to `solve.run` — exactly as if you had clicked each one in order. The Journal ends up ten Commands long again, this time for a 2 m beam, and the Results tab opens on its answer. You changed one character and re-ran the whole study.

steps.title: What a doubled length should do, and what makes any of this trustworthy
steps.explain: The arithmetic first, then the property that matters more than the arithmetic.
steps.theory:
Euler–Bernoulli deflection scales with the cube of the length: double $L$ and $\delta$ should scale by $2^3 = 8$. The original beam solved to $\delta = 0.1901\,\mathrm{mm}$; the edited script's 2 m beam solves to $\delta = 1.5196\,\mathrm{mm}$, against a predicted $8 \times 0.1901 = 1.5208\,\mathrm{mm}$ — 0.08 % low, an even better match than the 1 m beam's own 0.2 % gap to beam theory, which is what a more slender beam ($L/h = 20$ instead of $10$) should do to the shear-deflection term the formula leaves out.

**What makes this trustworthy rather than merely convenient.** A macro recorder gives you a click-path that repeats what a particular GUI happened to do; nothing checks that the replay is *correct*, only that it ran. A FEM Lab Journal is checked against itself: every entry carries `hashAfter`, a hash of the whole Model after that Command, and replaying the Journal anywhere recomputes it. That is exactly what the CLI's `--verify` flag does — and the ten Commands you built by hand in this tutorial are, Command for Command, the committed fixture at `crates/engine/benches/journals/cantilever.json`. From a terminal:
```
cargo run --release -p femlab -- run crates/engine/benches/journals/cantilever.json --verify --cpu
```
replays that exact file on the native engine — a different host from the wasm build this page runs on — and it fails loudly if even one recomputed hash disagrees with what is committed. `packages/app/test/tutorial-fixtures.test.ts` replays the same ten Commands through the wasm build on every CI run. A browser, the CLI and a server all read the same Journal the same way; that is not a claim about this codebase, it is one of the things CI checks on every push.
